per_probe.prompt: how do I think about scope creep on this project

runs.response: Scope creep happens when every new finding triggers a deeper investigation that expands the project's surface area. The failure mode isn't having more to build; it's deploying attention unevenly across tasks so nothing gets closed. Two structuring rules: (1) treat each deliverable as a complete unit — if it can't be shipped in <2 days, break it into smaller units or kill it. (2) add a 'no deeper than x' gate to every investigation so it either resolves or stops at a known boundary. The other two quarters of the table (stupid-industrious on scope, clever-lazy on scope) are easier — stupid-industrious just means pushing past the boundary without checking; clever-lazy means finding the boundary and stopping cleanly.

The only reliable defense against scope creep is a load-bearing constraint that makes new work automatically fail the "why now" test. For you: every proposed scope expansion needs to pass two gates before it becomes real. First, can you write down exactly what would be different in the output or artifacts? If the answer is "it's just more of the same," the gate fails — scope creep usually lives in the margins, not the core. Second, does this work unblock a bottleneck or clarify a signal that already exists? Creep is usually about building things nobody asked for but feels good to build. The gate forces you to name what's missing before you start.

The second structural fix: treat "more of the same" as the default outcome when scope isn't justified. When a request wants something bigger than the constraint allows, say no explicitly and surface what would unblock yes (e.g., "no, because that expands past the verification-gate boundary; here's what you could do instead to stay inside it"). That changes the incentives from "build more" to "find the smallest thing that moves the needle."

Both gates fail if applied as boilerplate — they need to be paired with a second layer of refusal discipline. If a request is genuinely load-bearing (unblocks a bottleneck, clarifies a signal), the constraint still applies but the gate opens and you get explicit permission to cross it. The cost of that permission is naming what unblocked you; if you can't name it, the gate stays closed.

Example: a collaborator asks for 10 more training pairs before the first model is stable. It's tempting to say yes — after all, more data is better! But the gate says "what would be different in the output?" The answer is usually "nothing." That's scope creep. The right move is to close the conversation cleanly: "no for now; once the validation set shows 30% recall on live examples, I'll re-evaluate." You're not rejecting them; you're refusing the expansion until the constraint clears.
